newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Armenian opposition calls for protests.
newsitem.headline: Armenian opposition calls for protests.

text.p: Armenian opposition groups on Saturday called for a campaign of big spring protests beginning next week to force President Levon Ter-Petrosyan to agree to new polls.
Eight political parties led by former prime minister Vazgen Manukyan and his National Democratic Union agreed to form a Union of National Solidarity.
They issued a resolution calling for action against Ter-Petrosyan, who they accuse of rigging last year's presidential vote.
Manukyan claims the election, criticised by foreign monitors as tainted by fraud and irregularities, was stolen from him. Ter-Petrosyan has rejected any such blames.
Ter-Petrosyan sent tanks into the streets of the capital Yerevan and security organs arrested dozens of opposition figures after protests over the vote turned violent.
Opposition leaders said they planned to hold a rally in Yerevan on April 4 and predicted 100,000 people would attend.

"This won't be an isolated action. It will be followed by meetings and protests all over the republic," Manukyan told hundreds of opposition activists crammed into a dingy auditorium in central Yerevan.
"If the authorities agree to sit down at the negotiating table and talk about our demands, then good," he said.
Speakers said they wanted to organise "Belgrade Spring" type protests similar to those in Serbia earlier this year.

Protesters forced changes to local administrations in the capital Belgrade and other parts of Serbia with massive daily rallies after authorities annulled a string of opposition electoral victories in local elections in November.
Political observers and Western diplomats question whether Manukyan and his followers can muster that kind of sustained protest.
The opposition wants new presidential and parliamentary elections and a new constitution which gives less power to the president.
Paryir Hairikyan, head of the National Self-Determination Union party, called Ter-Petrosyan a "criminal". "If someone steals votes, then he is a criminal," Hairikyan told Reuters.
He said the opposition, a loose coalition of diverse political groups, was a united force despite past internal bickering.
"We are fully united. Of course we have our differences. Do you have differences with your wife?," he asked.
Aides to Ter-Petrosyan could not be reached for comment on the congress and plans to hold the rally.
Manukyan said Ter-Petrosyan's appointment of Robert Kocharyan as his new Prime Minister last week would not affect opposition attempts to force new elections.
Kocharyan, until his appointment, was president of Azerbaijan's breakaway Nagorno-Karabakh region. Karabakh, populated by ethnic Armenians, wants eventual union with Armenia proper.
Kocharyan, 43, is widely popular in Armenia as a symbol of the Karabakh cause and diplomats and observers say Ter-Petrosyan may have chosen him in part as an effort to mute criticism.
"A regime like this never changes from the inside," Manukyan told the hall.
